newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault seeks 10-10.5 percent of European car sales.
newsitem.headline: Renault seeks 10-10.5 percent of European car sales.

text.p: French carmaker Renault, the smallest of Europe's Big Six car companies, aims to capture between 10 and 10.5 percent of western European car sales in 1997, sales director Patrick Faure said on Monday.
The company's market share slipped in 1996 to 10.1 percent from 10.3 percent the previous year due primarily to a drop in its share of the French car market.
Faure told reporters the group expected European car sales to rise slightly in 1997 as a result of a rebate incentive scheme introduced in Italy.

But Renault officials said they expected the French car market to shrink to around 1.9 million from 2.13 million in 1996, when a French state-sponsored rebate scheme underpinned the market for the first nine months of the year.
Renault aims to raise its share of the French car market to around 27-28 percent from 26.6 percent in 1996, representing 567,102 sales, Faure said. Its share was 29.2 percent in 1995.

"1997 will be the year of the reconquest. We have the products, the strategy and the sales team to do it," Faure told a news conference called to announce the group's 1996 sales. They rose to 1,475,453 vehicles last year from 1,439,686 in the previous year.
Faure said the group hoped the Megane car, ranked fourth in its segment in Europe in 1996 after the Volkswagen Golf, Opel Astra and Ford Escort, would be among the top three in 1997.
The Scenic version is selling well and new versions of the family will be rolled out in 1997.

Renault also hopes to recoup market share in Italy, where its prospects are helped by a recovery in the lira against the French franc and the new rebate scheme, Faure said. But he said the group would not go to extremes to win market share.
"As in France, the programme will probably skew sales toward smaller cars which isn't positive for carmakers' financial results," Faure said. Cheaper cars tend to have smaller margins.
He said there were no indications that a price war waged last year in Europe and centred in France was winding down.

The group said it aimed to expand its activities in fast-growing markets outside western Europe in 1997 and perhaps set up production in Russia with a partner. "Being among the first there would have its advantages," he said.
Renault's truck activity faces a tough year as several of its vehicles are nearing the end of the product life and their replacements will not be out before the end of the year.
"It'll be difficult. Some of our models are older than their competitors," Faure said.
Renault's share of the European industrial vehicle market fell to 13.7 percent in 1996 from 15.3 percent the previous year. Faure said it was aiming for a 13.5 percent share in 1997.
